Riding in January: The Hardest Month

January is the toughest month for UK motorcycle riding. Short days, cold temperatures, and unpredictable conditions test both rider and machine. But for those who brave it, the rewards are real — empty roads, crisp winter landscapes, and the quiet satisfaction of being a year-round rider.

What to Expect

  • Temperature: Average 2-7°C. Sub-zero mornings are common, especially inland. Wind chill on a motorcycle at 60mph can make 5°C feel like -10°C.
  • Daylight: Sunrise around 8am, sunset around 4pm. Useful riding hours are limited.
  • Road conditions: Salt, grit, and standing water are everywhere. Black ice is a genuine hazard, especially on shaded roads in the morning.
  • Weather: Rain, sleet, and occasional snow. Dry days exist but shouldn't be relied upon.

Essential January Gear

  • Heated grips: Non-negotiable for January riding. Cold hands lose feeling and dexterity, making braking and clutch control dangerous.
  • Heated vest or jacket: Powered from the bike's battery, these maintain core temperature even in freezing conditions.
  • Thermal base layers: Merino wool or technical thermal layers under your riding suit.
  • Winter gloves: Insulated, waterproof, with a long cuff to seal against drafts.
  • Pinlock visor insert: Stops visor fogging in cold, damp conditions. Essential for visibility.
  • Waterproof boots: Your feet will get cold and wet. Insulated, waterproof touring boots make a huge difference.

January Riding Tips

  • Ride during the warmest part of the day (11am-2pm) to minimise ice risk.
  • Avoid shaded roads in the morning — ice persists in shade when sunny sections are clear.
  • Stay off white lines, manhole covers, and painted road markings — they're lethal in the cold and wet.
  • Increase following distances. Cold tyres grip less, and braking distances increase in cold and wet conditions.
  • Wash your bike after every ride. Road salt is highly corrosive and will damage chain, frame, and fasteners.
January riding isn't about distance or speed — it's about maintaining your skills, keeping the battery charged, and enjoying the rare gift of empty roads. A 30-mile loop on a crisp January afternoon, with frost on the fields and clear winter light, is riding at its most elemental.

Where to Ride in January

  • Stick to lower-elevation roads — mountain passes may be closed or icy.
  • Coastal routes are often milder than inland — the sea moderates temperature.
  • Southern England is warmer than the north. Dorset, Devon, and Cornwall offer the most rideable January conditions.

January Maintenance

Use January's short days and cold temperatures productively. This is the ideal time for annual maintenance tasks — oil change, coolant flush, brake fluid replacement, and any repairs you've been putting off. A well-maintained bike is ready to go the moment spring arrives, rather than languishing in the garage while you wait for parts.

If you're storing your bike through January, ensure it's properly prepared: full tank (prevents internal corrosion), trickle charger connected, tyres inflated to recommended pressure, and a breathable cover to prevent condensation. faq.q: Is it safe to ride a motorcycle in January in the UK?
faq.a: Yes, but only with care. Ride during the warmest part of the day, roughly 11am to 2pm, when any overnight ice has cleared from sunlit sections. If the temperature is below 3C assume ice is possible, especially on shaded roads, bridges and painted markings. Empty roads and crisp winter light are the reward for those who prepare properly.

faq.q: What gear do I need for January riding?
faq.a: Heated grips are essential because cold hands lose the dexterity needed for safe braking and clutch control. Add a battery-powered heated vest or jacket, merino or technical thermal base layers, insulated waterproof winter gloves with long cuffs, waterproof boots and a Pinlock visor insert to stop fogging. Cold, wet feet and misted vision ruin January rides faster than anything else.

faq.q: How do I stop road salt damaging my bike in January?
faq.a: Wash your bike after every winter ride. Road salt is highly corrosive and attacks the chain, frame and fasteners quickly. Rinse thoroughly, dry the bike, then apply a corrosion protectant such as ACF-50 to bare metal and electrical connections. Keeping the chain well lubricated is also vital because gritty winter roads strip lube rapidly.

faq.q: Where are the best places to ride in January?
faq.a: Stick to lower-elevation roads because mountain passes may be icy or closed. Coastal routes tend to be milder than inland as the sea moderates temperature. Southern England is warmer than the north, so Dorset, Devon and Cornwall offer the most rideable January conditions. Keep rides short and purposeful rather than chasing big distances.

faq.q: Should I store my bike or keep riding in January?
faq.a: Either works if done properly. January is an ideal time for annual maintenance such as an oil change, coolant flush and brake fluid replacement. If storing, fill the tank to prevent internal corrosion, connect a trickle charger, inflate tyres to the recommended pressure and use a breathable cover. A monthly check catches problems before spring.
